strengths: Broad and useful contribution: curating 144 diverse reasoning/planning tasks into a unified, automatically gradeable format for training and evaluating Code Interpreter–augmented LLMs, with datasets, code, and models promised to be released, which is a valuable resource for the community.

The paper is one of the first to systematically study RL-based training of a general-purpose (not math-only) Code Interpreter across heterogeneous tasks, and clearly documents why vanilla DeepSeek-style GRPO fails in this setting (sparse effective samples, task heterogeneity).

The multi-stage curriculum guided by measured 'improvement potential' is well motivated, empirically effective (RL gains rise from +3.4% to +9.3%), and supported by a simple but coherent theoretical analysis (Appendix C) showing the GRPO policy signal vanishes for near-deterministic success/failure items.

Extensive ablations: multi-turn CI vs. All-Text/All-Code frameworks, warm vs. cold start, curriculum vs. difficulty-based ordering vs. no curriculum, and Qwen-2.5 vs. DeepSeek-distilled base models — these collectively support the design choices rather than just the final system.

Practical systems contribution: decoupling code execution from GPU training via a CPU sandbox yields a substantial ~39% training-time reduction and addresses a real bottleneck (sparse GPU utilization) that is under-documented in prior tool-integrated RL work.
Results are strong and reported across three model sizes (3B/7B/14B) with consistent trends; RI-CI-14B surpasses GPT-4o with and without Code Interpreter on their test suite.
Interesting behavioral analysis, e.g., emergent self-checking via code, code usage turn distributions, and the observation that response length does not grow during RL here.
weaknesses: Evaluation generalization is limited: all 37 test tasks come from the same three benchmark families (SymBench, Big-Bench-Hard, Reasoning-Gym) as the 107 training tasks, with the same unified format and rule-based grading. There is no held-out out-of-distribution evaluation (e.g., fresh benchmarks, different answer formats), so claims of 'generalization' may mostly reflect in-distribution generalization.

The GPT-4o baseline comparison is somewhat circular: SFT data are 6.5k GPT-4o-generated trajectories, and GPT-4o also assists in answer format normalization during evaluation. Surpassing GPT-4o on a suite largely covered by GPT-4o-distilled training data weakens the headline claim.

Novelty is moderate: the 'improvement potential' ordering is essentially an empirical-variance/p(1−p) heuristic (train on samples the model gets right ~50% of the time), which is a well-known intuition in RL and curriculum learning; the theoretical analysis in Appendix C is a straightforward Bernoulli-variance/Cauchy–Schwarz argument. Related tool-integrated RL works (ToRL, ReTool, ToQL, Search-R1) are dismissed as 'math-only' but the delta should be more carefully argued.

Single-run experiments with no variance estimates, seeds, or significance testing; curriculum stage length (150 steps) and four-stage partitioning appear chosen by hand, and sensitivity to these hyperparameters is not explored.

Some inconsistencies and unsupported claims: Table 2 is described as 'four pre-designed agents' but captioned '15 agents'; the 'first published work to train general Code Interpreter' claim is stated too strongly given contemporaneous tool-integrated RL work; 'emergent' self-checking is measured by GPT-4o judgments, which is a noisy and potentially biased proxy.

The RL signal is essentially outcome-only (exact match / rule check) with small format/efficiency bonuses; no comparison to outcome-only RL without the efficiency penalties, and the weighted reward design is not ablated.

Compute and cost reporting are appreciated but the paper would benefit from comparing token/inference cost against the baselines explicitly, since multi-turn execution naturally uses more tokens; the current discussion is qualitative.
Reproducibility of the full pipeline depends on closed models (GPT-4o for trajectory synthesis and judging) and proprietary benchmarks, which limits independent verification despite the code release.

strengths: Broad empirical scope: curating 144 reasoning/planning tasks from three benchmarks into a unified, rule-verifiable format is a useful contribution for the community, and the models/datasets/code are stated to be released, aiding reproducibility.

The paper identifies and documents a real phenomenon (vanilla GRPO yielding marginal gains on heterogeneous multi-task tool-use data) and supports it with both empirical curves (Fig. 3) and a simple variance analysis (Lemma C.1, Prop. 1) explaining why near-zero-variance samples produce weak policy signal.

The improvement-potential metric (Π_i = 4p(1-p)) is a sensible, theoretically motivated sample-difficulty measure, and the ablations (R1-CI wo CL, wo IP, wo GRPO) across three model sizes reasonably isolate the contribution of the curriculum.

The decoupled CPU Code Execution Sandbox is a practical systems contribution with a quantified 39% training-time reduction, and response-characteristic analyses (self-checking, code-usage turns, response length) add useful insight.
Honest cost reporting (1845 GPU-hours) and several useful training-strategy comparisons (warm vs. cold start, Qwen vs. DeepSeek-distilled bases).
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to tasks drawn from the same three benchmark families used for training (SymBench, Big-Bench-Hard, Reasoning-Gym), with a train/test split over task types. There is no out-of-distribution evaluation on standard held-out benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, AIME, GPQA, LiveCodeBench), so the central claim of a 'general-purpose' Code Interpreter with 'broad effectiveness' is only weakly supported; generalization across task categories within the same suites does not establish generality.

Limited novelty of the core method: curriculum ordering by empirical pass rate/variance is close to known ideas (pass-rate filtering, dynamic sampling in DAPO-style pipelines, hard-example mining), and the theoretical analysis (Bernoulli variance identity + Cauchy–Schwarz bound) is elementary; the bounds concern gradient magnitude rather than actual learning progress, and the gap between the bound and the empirical curriculum benefit is not tightly justified.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o distillation for SFT trajectories (6.5k trajectories) and GPT-4o judging for the 'emergent self-checking' analysis; the latter claim in particular rests on GPT-4o-based classification of trajectories rather than human verification, and comparisons against GPT-4o (a likely teacher) should be interpreted with care.

The improvement-potential estimation is expensive (N=20 rollouts across 4 agent frameworks per training question) and its cost/benefit versus simply using pass-rate difficulty or prior dynamic-sampling heuristics is not quantified; the 'wo IP' ablation uses question difficulty, but other cheaper proxies are not explored.

Several presentation issues undermine polish: the abstract's release URL is missing ('available at and'), Table 2 header says '15 agents' but lists 4, Appendix D (Ablation Study) is essentially empty, and the training-vs-test task split rationale is thin.
Only Qwen-2.5 base models are studied in depth; the DeepSeek comparison (Table 4) is limited to a few configurations, leaving open how the method transfers to other model families or larger scales.

Reward design details (format compliance, turn-count penalties) introduce tunable knobs whose sensitivity is not ablated, and the possibility of reward hacking of rule-based verifiers in some of the 144 tasks is not discussed.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: training a general-purpose Code Interpreter-augmented LLM across many diverse tasks, rather than a single domain (math/retrieval), which distinguishes it from ToRL, ReTool, and similar tool-integrated RL work.

The empirical finding that vanilla GRPO yields marginal gains (+3.4%) on heterogeneous tasks is well-motivated and supported by a clean theoretical analysis (Appendix C) showing that the policy-gradient signal vanishes for samples with p near 0 or 1 via a Bernoulli variance identity and Cauchy-Schwarz bound. This gives the curriculum design a principled justification rather than being purely heuristic.

The improvement-potential metric (Π_i = 4p_i(1-p_i)) is a simple but sensible criterion for ordering curriculum samples, and the ablations (R1-CI wo CL, wo IP, difficulty-calibrated curriculum) across three model sizes consistently support the claimed contribution.

Comprehensive evaluation: 144 tasks from three benchmark suites with a train/test split, comparisons against multiple prompting baselines (All Text, All Code, Code Agent, CodeSteer), GPT-4o text-only and GPT-4o + Code Interpreter, and careful attention to fairness (same GPT-4o SFT data budget for All Text/All Code).

Practical systems contribution: the Code Execution Sandbox that decouples CPU-based code execution from GPU gradient computation reduces training time by 39% (4500 to 1845 GPU hours), a non-trivial engineering result useful to practitioners.
Interesting analysis of emergent self-checking behavior and response-length dynamics (no length growth, unlike prior RL findings), with plausible explanations.
Claims reproducibility via released datasets, code, and models, and reports sufficient training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Limited task novelty: the 144 tasks are compiled from existing benchmarks (SymBench, Big-Bench-Hard, Reasoning-Gym) with only format standardization; the contribution is the training methodology rather than a new capability or benchmark. Test generalization is confined to 37 held-out tasks drawn from the same three suites, so out-of-distribution generalization is not demonstrated.

The core curriculum idea (ordering training samples by success-rate variance p(1-p)) is fairly incremental; similar dynamic sampling / filtering ideas exist in prior RL work (e.g., DAPO-style filtering of zero-variance groups), and the paper does not thoroughly position or compare against sample-filtering alternatives within GRPO itself.

Improvement potential is estimated with only N=20 samples across four agent variants before training; the estimator's noise at this scale and its sensitivity to the number of samples/stages are not ablated. Stage boundaries and the 150-step stage schedule appear hand-tuned without sensitivity analysis.

Potential confound in the headline comparison: R1-CI is trained with GPT-4o-generated SFT data and evaluated on tasks whose evaluation relies on rule-based matching; the comparison to GPT-4o (text-only) may partly reflect task-format familiarity rather than genuine symbolic reasoning gains. No variance across random seeds or confidence intervals is reported anywhere in the tables.

The theoretical analysis assumes i.i.d. Bernoulli rewards per sample and ignores clipping; while acknowledged, the gap between theory (signal vanishing) and the empirical curriculum gains (+3.4% → +9.3%) is not fully connected, e.g., no measurement of realized gradient norms or ψ(B) during actual training to validate Proposition 1/2 in practice.

Statistical reporting is thin: single runs per configuration, no error bars, and some results (e.g., R1-CI-3B barely beating R1-CI-3B wo IP on test: 58.0 vs 53.4 but below SFT-only variant on some splits) suggest high variance that is not discussed.

Some ablations are relegated to the appendix in brief form (Appendix D is essentially empty as a section header), and the DeepSeek-distilled base model comparison is limited to a single table without full RL training.

Writing has minor issues: the abstract's release URL is incomplete ('available at and'), Figure 1b/4a appear nearly duplicated, and some claims (e.g., 'first published work to train general Code Interpreter across multiple tasks') are strong and hard to verify.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: the paper trains a general-purpose Code Interpreter across 144 diverse reasoning/planning tasks with 200+ samples each, evaluating three model sizes (3/7/14B), multiple baselines (All Text, All Code, Code Agent, CodeSteer, GPT-4o with/without CI), and extensive ablations (RL algorithm choice, warm vs. cold start, offline vs. online curriculum, SFT dataset design, second RL round, base model choice).

Clear and useful problem identification: the paper convincingly demonstrates, both empirically (Fig. 3, task-count scaling) and theoretically (variance of group-relative Bernoulli rewards is maximized at p=0.5), why vanilla GRPO stalls on heterogeneous task mixtures—a valuable and reproducible negative/analysis result for the community.

The improvement-potential curriculum is well-motivated, formally linked to the gradient-magnitude analysis (Prop. 1-2, App. D), and validated directly (Fig. 14 shows higher-potential groups yield larger gains; ablation vs. difficulty-based curriculum).

Strong headline results: R1-CI-14B (72.4%) outperforms both text-only GPT-4o (58.6%) and GPT-4o with its native Code Interpreter (70.9%) on 37 held-out tasks, with consistent gains across model sizes; OOD evaluations (GPQA, AIME, BBH-as-OOD) support generalization.

Practical systems contribution: decoupling code execution into a CPU sandbox reduces RL training time by ~39%, and the paper transparently reports substantial training cost (1845 GPU-hours), which is rare and helpful.

Good analysis of emergent behaviors (self-checking via code, code-usage turn distribution, response-length non-inflation) and clear reproducibility plans (code, data, models to be released; detailed task descriptions in appendix).
weaknesses: Moderate conceptual novelty: the core technique—ordering RL samples by success-rate variance (p(1-p))—is close to known ideas in difficulty-aware curriculum RL and dynamic sample filtering (e.g., DAPO-style filtering, hard-example mining); the paper would benefit from a more explicit comparison to and differentiation from such prior data-selection methods for RL.

Test tasks come from the same three benchmarks (37 tasks split off from the same 144), so train/test tasks are highly distributionally similar; results over 37 tasks may also have notable variance. OOD results are relegated to the appendix and cover only GPQA/AIME and one leave-one-benchmark-out setting.

The theoretical analysis, while correct, is elementary (Bernoulli variance identity plus Cauchy-Schwarz); it supports the method but does not constitute a deep contribution, and assumptions (i.i.d. Bernoulli rewards, ignoring clipping, per-token v_i independence) are somewhat idealized.

Improvement-potential estimation is costly (4 agent variants × 5 samples = 20 rollouts per question, plus multi-turn code execution) and measured with the post-SFT model; the paper does not quantify how noisy these estimates are or how sensitive results are to N and group thresholds.

The improvement over difficulty-based curriculum (R1-CI vs. R1-CI wo IP: 66.4 vs. 72.4 on test) is significant but the ablation of number of curriculum stages (4) and alternative potential estimators is absent.

SFT data is distilled entirely from GPT-4o, and GPT-4o is also used for answer-format normalization and judging self-checking behavior—this entangles the results with GPT-4o's capabilities and introduces potential evaluation bias; prior tool-RL works (ToRL, ReTool) are motivated and compared qualitatively but not reproduced head-to-head.
Base models are Qwen2.5-Instruct series, which is somewhat dated relative to current reasoning-capable open models; the DeepSeek-distilled comparison (App. G) is limited to SFT-level results.

Some claims are overstated (e.g., 'first published work to train general Code Interpreter across multiple tasks and domains'—the boundary with ToRL/ReTool/ToolRL needs more careful qualification), and a few result details (e.g., exact reward weights, evaluation protocols for GPT-4o CI baseline) are only sketched.

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark construction: 144 diverse reasoning/planning tasks compiled from three sources with a unified rollout/evaluation format, spanning multiple capability categories; this is a useful resource for the community.

Extensive empirical evaluation: results across three model sizes (3B/7B/14B), comparisons against multiple prompting baselines (All Text, All Code, Code Agent, CodeSteer), GPT-4o references, and an unusually broad set of ablations (RL algorithm choice, warm vs. cold start, online vs. offline curriculum, SFT dataset design, OOD generalization).

The proposed improvement-potential curriculum is well-motivated: the appendix provides a clean analysis linking GRPO gradient magnitude to Bernoulli reward variance p(1-p), and the Fig. 14/Fig. 3d experiments empirically support that high-potential samples yield larger gains.

Honest reporting of negative findings: the paper documents that vanilla GRPO yields only marginal gains (+3.4%) on heterogeneous task mixtures, and that final-stage low-potential samples contribute little, which is informative for practitioners.
Practical systems contribution: decoupling code execution onto CPU sandboxes to reduce RL training time by ~39% is a nontrivial and useful engineering result.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method. Ranking samples by success-rate variance p(1-p) is an intuitive and fairly straightforward idea, closely related to existing difficulty/pass-rate filtering and dynamic sampling in RL for LLMs (e.g., DAPO's approach to degenerate groups). The multi-stage curriculum is a reasonable but incremental extension; the theoretical analysis is elementary (variance identity plus Cauchy-Schwarz).

Heavy dependence on GPT-4o distillation. SFT trajectories are entirely GPT-4o-generated, evaluation uses GPT-4o for format normalization, and the 'emergent self-checking' claim is verified by prompting GPT-4o to classify trajectories. This raises questions about how much of the gain is genuine learned behavior versus distillation of GPT-4o's tool-use patterns, and the self-checking evidence is qualitative/LLM-judged rather than rigorous.

Overstated claims: 'first published work to train general Code Interpreter' is contestable given prior tool-integrated RL work; 'emergent self-checking' is a strong claim supported mainly by an LLM-based annotation. The improvement of the full method over SFT-only (+12 points) is largely attributable to the SFT stage (44.1 -> 60.1), with the curriculum/RL machinery contributing a smaller increment (60.1 -> 72.4).

Missing direct comparisons with closest prior work: ToRL and ReTool are cited as the closest tool-integrated RL methods but are not evaluated or adapted as baselines on this benchmark, making it hard to judge whether the curriculum framework is superior to simply scaling those approaches.

Scalability and cost concerns: the improvement-potential estimation requires 20 rollouts per training sample (four agent variants x five temperatures) before training, and RL training still costs ~1845 GPU hours for the 14B model; the paper does not analyze whether the potential-estimation overhead is justified relative to simpler difficulty-based ranking (the wo IP ablation is only a 6-point gap and potentially confounded by cutoff choices).

Evaluation design details are under-specified: sample selection across tasks (200+ samples each, up to 70 SFT trajectories), how the 37 test tasks were chosen, statistical significance/variance of reported averages, and handling of the 60-second execution timeout, which appears to substantially affect planning tasks. Only OOD Table 4 reports averages over repeated runs; the main table appears to be single-run.

The claim that RL gains are marginal due to 'task heterogeneity' is supported by a gradient-magnitude argument but alternative explanations (e.g., verifier noise, format reward shaping, max-turns penalty) are not controlled for, weakening the causal attribution.

strengths: Substantial and useful contribution in scope: the paper curates 144 diverse reasoning and planning tasks (from SymBench, BBH, Reasoning-Gym) in a unified, automatically verifiable format, and provides the first systematic study of training a general-purpose Code Interpreter with SFT + GRPO across many task types rather than a single math domain.

The core finding—that vanilla GRPO yields only +3.4% on heterogeneous multi-task data—is well motivated and supported by both empirical evidence (Fig. 3, single-task vs. 107-task scaling) and a clean theoretical analysis (Lemma D.1 / Prop. 1 showing the policy-gradient signal scales with p(1-p) and vanishes on too-easy/too-hard items).

The multi-stage curriculum ordered by measured improvement potential (Π = 4p(1-p)) is a sensible, principled remedy, and the ablation against difficulty-based calibration (R1-CI wo IP) and Fig. 14 directly validate the mechanism rather than just the final result.

Comprehensive evaluation: results across three model sizes (3/7/14B), comparisons to GPT-4o text-only and GPT-4o+Code Interpreter, OOD evaluation (GPQA, AIME, BBH held out), and extensive ablations (warm vs. cold start, RL algorithm choice, offline vs. online curriculum, RL rounds, SFT data design, base model choice).
Practical engineering contribution: decoupling code execution into a CPU sandbox reduces training time by ~39%, an analysis (GPU utilization, Fig. 12) that is useful for practitioners.
The paper is generally well written, with clear formulation of the training objective and reproducibility details (hyperparameters, GPU hours, prompt format, full task descriptions in Appendix H).
weaknesses: Novelty of the central technique is moderate: ordering RL training data by pass-rate-based variance (p(1-p)) is closely related to known practices—dynamic sampling of near-50%-pass-rate prompts (e.g., DAPO), pass-rate filtering in tool-integrated RL, and prior curriculum learning by difficulty. The paper's framing as a 'novel' contribution overstates the delta; the main novelty is applying it to a general Code Interpreter setting.

Improvement-potential estimation is expensive and somewhat ad hoc: it requires 20 extra sampled answers per question across four different agent frameworks (including a CodeSteer run, which itself needs a separate steering agent). The paper does not analyze the sensitivity of results to N=20, to the choice of agent variants, or to the arbitrary four-stage partition thresholds ([0,0.32],[0.32,0.48], etc.).

The GRPO stage adds relatively modest gains over SFT alone (e.g., 60.1→72.4 on test for 14B, but only 48.0→58.0 for 3B), and curriculum learning adds ~6 points over difficulty-based calibration for 14B but less for smaller models (53.4→58.0, 62.7→66.6). The headline claims should be tempered accordingly; error bars / significance tests are absent from the main table despite presumably large per-task variance.

Baseline comparisons to GPT-4o are somewhat dated: GPT-4o is no longer the strongest reference model; comparisons to GPT-4o with Code Interpreter (70.9% vs. 72.4%) are close and the paper does not discuss inference-cost differences fairly (R1-CI requires multi-turn generation, up to 8 code calls, ~2 minutes per question).

Evaluation is rule-based with GPT-4o assisting 'format normalization when necessary'—this introduces potential evaluation noise or leakage concerns, and inter-annotator/automated-judge reliability is not quantified.
Emergent self-checking behavior is characterized only by a GPT-4o-judged proportion of trajectories (Fig. 6a); a more careful qualitative or causal analysis would strengthen this interesting claim.
Some OOD results (AIME 24&25 with 30-42%) come from small test sets averaged over three runs; confidence intervals are not reported, and per-benchmark breakdown of the OOD numbers is not provided.
